title: The first room after death: staying, calling, rituals, and the body

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe recognized patterns but do not supply firsthand room texture.
The record must not be used to diagnose, time, or manage a particular death.
Treatment, legal, ritual, and emergency decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: After the person has died, those present may sit with the body, call staff or a care team, contact family, begin ritual or practical steps, and face the first shift from caring for a living person to caring for a dead body and the bereaved.
ordinary_language_queries: what do I do after someone dies at home hospice
can I sit with the body after death
who do I call when they die at home

content_layers.observation_text: Public sources describe that families may wish to stay with the person after death, that cultural or religious practices may matter, and that practical steps depend on setting and jurisdiction.
content_layers.source_synthesis: NCI, Marie Curie, Marie Curie professional care-after-death guidance, and healthdirect support a cautious after-death record centered on dignity, wishes, support, and local next steps.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This record is the first bridge from dying to aftermath. It marks the “second threshold”: not the last breath, but the first call, the first waiting, the first body-care decisions.

what_this_is_not: not a legal checklist for all jurisdictions
not a substitute for local hospice, medical, funeral, cultural, or legal guidance
not a claim that every family should stay with the body
uncertainties: Legal requirements vary sharply by place.
Home, hospital, hospice, care-home, custody, and sudden-death settings require different pathways.
The corpus needs funeral director, nurse, chaplain, and family testimony.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should say that there is often no need to rush emotionally, but practical calls and legal steps are local; use the care plan, hospice number, GP/doctor, facility staff, or emergency pathways as appropriate.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect the choreography of the first hour after death: who speaks, who calls, who washes, who waits, who removes equipment, and who protects dignity.
language_notes: Do not universalize UK or Australian administrative steps.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the v2 witnessed-moment schema. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical safety review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent or worried readers to qualified local support.
